lessons.title: Why AI matters — and why you stay in charge
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I use AI, and what do I keep deciding myself?
lessons.blurb: Start from your choices, not the hype. Set one rule you can keep.

resources.label: Elements of AI — free intro course

steps.title: You see this every week
steps.scenario: One friend uses AI and their grades go up. Another says AI is dangerous and refuses to touch it. A third uses it for literally everything. They are all talking at once.
steps.prompt: Before reading on: in one sentence, what would YOUR rule be?

steps.title: Sort these uses
steps.prompt: Which of these keep you learning, and which quietly replace your thinking?

items.text: Ask AI to explain a concept, then re-explain it back in your own words
Paste the homework question and copy the answer
Ask for 3 angles on an essay, then pick and argue one yourself
Let AI write the whole essay and submit it

steps.reveal: The line is not "AI or no AI." It is "did I still do the thinking that matters?"

steps.title: Agency is the real skill
steps.body: AI is useful when a human keeps the goal, the method, and the verification. Speed is not the same as understanding.
steps.mistake: Trusting a fluent answer because it sounds confident.
steps.good: Use AI to improve your reasoning, and skip it when it tempts you to stop thinking.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I am deciding when AI helps me without replacing my thinking. Give me 5 useful use cases and 5 risky shortcuts for someone like me. For each risky shortcut, add one question I should ask myself before using it.
steps.note: Run this in any free AI tool, then keep the 5 risky ones near your desk.

fields.label: I want AI to help me…
I will not let AI decide…
Before I trust it, I will check…

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which is the strongest reason to keep a human in charge?

options.text: AI is always wrong
options.feedback: Too strong — AI is often useful. The issue is unverified trust.

options.text: A fluent answer can still be wrong or low-value
options.feedback: Exactly. Confidence is not proof.

options.text: Using AI is against the rules
options.feedback: Not the point — many uses are fine when you stay in charge.

lessons.title: Your first useful AI conversation
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I frame a request so the answer is useful and checkable?
lessons.blurb: A good conversation is a loop, not one-shot magic.

steps.title: Ten minutes, something hard
steps.scenario: You are stuck on photosynthesis with a quiz tomorrow. You want help, but you do not want to just copy and understand nothing.
steps.prompt: What is the first thing you would type?

steps.title: Two ways to ask
steps.strong: You are my tutor. I am studying photosynthesis for a quiz. Ask me one question first, give one hint, then explain simply. Make me try one example before you give the full answer.
steps.why: The strong version sets a role, context, structure, and a required learner check — so the AI coaches instead of dumping an answer.

steps.title: Repair a weak prompt
steps.strong: Goal: understand the water cycle well enough to teach it. Context: I am in 9th grade and confused about condensation vs. evaporation. Constraints: simple words, no jargon without a definition. Format: 4 short steps, then 2 quiz questions for me.

steps.title: Make a loop, not a dump
steps.body: A useful request includes role, context, what help you want, and what the AI should NOT do for you.
steps.mistake: Accepting a full answer immediately, without your own attempt.
steps.good: Ask for a short output first, then a follow-up after you try.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Act like a peer tutor for [your topic]. Ask what I already understand, give one hint, then wait for my attempt. Only after I try, give your fuller explanation.
steps.note: Swap in a topic you actually have due this week.

fields.label: A check I will do first
fields.placeholder: try one example before the answer

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What made the strong prompt better?

options.text: It was longer
options.feedback: Length alone is not it — vague long prompts still fail.

options.text: It gave role, context, and a required check
options.feedback: Yes — structure creates a coaching loop.

options.text: It used bigger words
options.feedback: No — it asked for simpler words, in fact.

lessons.title: What AI actually is
lessons.coreQuestion: What is AI really doing, under the confident tone?
lessons.blurb: A pattern system, not a human mind. That frame keeps your options open.

steps.title: "It understands everything"
steps.scenario: A classmate insists the AI "just knows" the answer because it sounds so sure.
steps.prompt: Do you buy it? Why or why not?

steps.title: Which frame holds up?
steps.prompt: Tag each statement as a useful frame or a misconception.

items.text: AI is trained software that generates patterns from data
AI thinks like a human and is almost always right
AI is a perfect, live library lookup
AI is great for fast drafts I then verify

steps.reveal: Patterns are powerful but not infallible. A polished paragraph can still be invented.

steps.title: Generate first, verify always
steps.body: AI is strong at generating language patterns fast. That gives you drafts and ideas quickly.
steps.good: Use AI for options, then test each against your own understanding and a source.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Explain what AI is to a 14-year-old in 3 plain lines, without saying it is "smart like a person." Then give me 2 trap questions I can use to check whether a definition is too naive.
steps.note: Use the trap questions on a friend — or on yourself.

fields.label: So I will verify…
fields.placeholder: any fact I would repeat out loud

options.text: Software that recognizes and generates patterns from data
options.feedback: Practical and honest.

options.text: A mind that understands like a person
options.feedback: Overstated — leads to trust mistakes.

options.text: A search engine that is always right
options.feedback: No — it generates, and can invent.

lessons.title: What an LLM is, without the magic
lessons.coreQuestion: Why is it so fluent, and why can it still be confidently wrong?
lessons.blurb: Tokens, context, and likely next words become your control points.

steps.title: Fluent, and still wrong
steps.scenario: Your model writes a smooth paragraph but skips one requirement you clearly stated.
steps.prompt: What do you think happened inside?

steps.title: Predict the next word
steps.note: An LLM picks likely next tokens from context. Fluency comes from "what usually follows," not from looking anything up.

steps.title: Context is the steering wheel
steps.body: An LLM predicts likely next tokens given your context and its training. If a key constraint is missing or buried, output drifts — confidently.
steps.mistake: Assuming it "remembers" everything like a person.
steps.good: State constraints explicitly, set an output format, and ask for a self-check.

steps.title: Where it goes wrong
steps.weak: Write about the French Revolution. (then later) Also keep it under 100 words.
steps.strong: In under 100 words, write about the French Revolution for a 9th grader. End by listing the 2 facts I should double-check.
steps.why: Front-loading the constraint and asking for a verification list fights the "drift" you just saw.

steps.title: Repair the prompt so context stays visible
steps.strong: Explain photosynthesis to someone like me in under 120 words. Use one concrete analogy, define glucose, and end with 2 facts I should verify in a biology source.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Give me one 2-minute exercise that teaches a friend the difference between fluency and truth, using a single AI answer as the example.
steps.note: Bonus: run the exercise and see if they get fooled.

fields.label: I will keep context visible by...
fields.placeholder: putting the goal and audience first

fields.label: I will prevent drift by...
fields.placeholder: setting length, format, and must-include details

fields.label: I will check truth by...
fields.placeholder: asking what to verify outside the model

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Why can an LLM be fluent but wrong?

options.text: It predicts likely text, which is not the same as verified fact
options.feedback: Right — likelihood ≠ truth.

options.text: It is broken
options.feedback: No — this is normal behavior to design around.

options.text: It is lying on purpose
options.feedback: No intent — it has no notion of truth unless you add tools/checks.

lessons.title: Prompt repair: goal, context, constraints, format
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a weak ask into a useful instruction?
lessons.blurb: The difference between asking and prompting — a repeatable repair.

steps.title: Boring answer again
steps.scenario: Same question, but the answer comes back generic and useless. The question was not the problem — the prompt was.
steps.prompt: What is one thing you would add to fix it?

steps.title: Repair it live
steps.strong: Goal: a study summary I can revise from tonight. Context: 10th-grade biology, cell division, quiz Friday. Constraints: no homework answers given away; define any term you use. Format: 3 key ideas, 1 common mistake, and a 2-question self-quiz.

steps.title: Prompts are instructions
steps.body: A prompt is executable instruction, not a wish. Better structure → more control.
steps.mistake: A polished sentence with an unclear goal still fails.
steps.good: Keep the goal concrete, constraints explicit, and ask for a quick self-check from the AI.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is my prompt: "[paste your weak prompt]". Rewrite it using Goal, Context, Constraints, Format. Then show me the improved answer and tell me which change mattered most.
steps.note: Compare the before/after — keep the diff in your toolkit.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which piece most often fixes a vague prompt first?

options.text: A concrete goal
options.feedback: Usually yes — without it, everything else floats.

options.text: More polite wording
options.feedback: Politeness does not add control.

options.text: Making it longer
options.feedback: Length without structure does not help.

lessons.title: Data, training & patterns
lessons.coreQuestion: Where does an AI’s “knowledge” come from?
lessons.blurb: Training turns examples into patterns. Useful, but not the same as knowing.

resources.label: Elements of AI — machine learning basics

steps.title: It feels like it just knows
steps.scenario: You ask an AI for a study plan, a poem, and a history summary. It answers all three like it has seen the inside of every classroom.
steps.prompt: Where do you think that ability came from?

steps.title: Training source or live fact?
steps.prompt: Sort what comes from training patterns versus what would need a current source or tool.

items.text: Writing a sentence that sounds like a lab report
Knowing whether your school canceled practice today
Recognizing that "photosynthesis" belongs with plants and light
Checking the exact deadline on your teacher’s website

steps.reveal: Training gives the model patterns. Current facts need a current source, a tool, or your own check.

steps.title: Patterns become predictions
steps.stem: In a recipe, after "preheat the oven to" you often see
steps.note: The model is not opening a cookbook. It has learned which kinds of text usually follow other text.

steps.title: Training is pattern learning
steps.body: AI systems are trained on lots of examples so they can predict, classify, or generate new outputs that match patterns in those examples.
steps.mistake: Treating training data like a perfect memory bank or a live database.
steps.good: Use AI for pattern-heavy work, then verify any fact, quote, date, rule, or local detail.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Explain training data to me using one school analogy and one sports or arts analogy. Then list 5 things a trained model can do well and 5 things I should verify somewhere else.
steps.note: Keep the verify list. It is the practical part.

fields.label: I can use AI for patterns like...
My first source check will be...

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the safest way to describe training?

options.text: The model memorizes a perfect copy of every fact
options.feedback: No. Training learns patterns, and outputs can still be wrong.

options.text: The model learns patterns from examples, then generates from those patterns
options.feedback: Exactly. That is useful, but it still needs verification.

options.text: The model searches the web every time it answers
options.feedback: Not by default. Some AI tools can use search, but the model itself generates.

lessons.title: Context windows & memory
lessons.coreQuestion: What does the AI actually remember, and for how long?
lessons.blurb: The model responds to what is in the current context. Memory is not magic.

steps.title: "But I already told it"
steps.scenario: You told an AI your project rules at the start. Ten messages later, it ignores one and gives advice that breaks the assignment.
steps.prompt: Did it forget, miss the rule, or never really remember like a person?

steps.title: In context or out of reach?
steps.prompt: Sort what the AI can use right now versus what you need to restate or provide again.

items.text: A rubric you pasted two messages ago
A file you never uploaded or pasted
A constraint buried 40 messages back in a long chat
The format you put in the prompt it is answering now

steps.reveal: If it matters, keep it visible. Important instructions belong near the task, not buried.

steps.title: Move the rule into view
steps.weak: Make this better but remember my teacher’s rules from before.
steps.strong: Goal: improve my paragraph without changing my argument. Context: 10th-grade English, persuasive paragraph. Constraints: keep my voice, do not add outside facts, and follow this rubric: [paste rubric]. Format: return a revised paragraph plus 3 notes explaining what changed.

steps.title: Context is working memory
steps.body: A context window is the information the model can use for the current response. Some products add saved memory, but you should not assume it has the exact thing you meant.
steps.mistake: Saying "you know what I mean" when the instruction is not visible.
steps.good: Restate the goal, paste key constraints, and ask the AI to repeat the rules before it works.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Before helping me, summarize the constraints I gave you in 3 bullets. If any constraint is missing or unclear, ask me a question instead of guessing. Then complete the task.
steps.note: This works especially well when a rubric or teacher rule matters.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What should you do when a rule really matters?

options.text: Assume the AI remembers it from earlier
options.feedback: Risky. Earlier context can be missed, compressed, or absent.

options.text: Put the rule close to the task and ask the AI to confirm it
options.feedback: Right. Keep important context visible.

options.text: Start a brand-new chat for every sentence
options.feedback: Not necessary. The point is to manage context, not avoid conversation.

lessons.title: Why AI hallucinates
lessons.coreQuestion: Why does it invent things — and how do I catch it?
lessons.blurb: A confident answer can be a guess wearing a suit. Learn the catch routine.

resources.label: Common Sense Media — AI and misinformation

steps.title: The fake quote problem
steps.scenario: An AI gives you a perfect-looking quote for an essay. The wording is strong, the author sounds right, and the citation looks real.
steps.prompt: What would you check before using it?

steps.title: Safe to use or verify first?
steps.prompt: Sort each AI output by what you should do next.

items.text: Three possible titles for your presentation
A quote supposedly from a scientist
A made-up practice problem for algebra
A statistic about teen phone use in 2026

steps.reveal: Ideas can be useful without being true. Claims need proof.

steps.title: Run a hallucination check
steps.claim: A famous researcher said, "AI literacy is the new oxygen of education."
steps: Copy the exact quote into a search engine with quotation marks.
Search the person’s official page or a reliable publication, not only random quote sites.
If you cannot find the quote in a trustworthy place, do not use it as real.
Ask the AI for a safer replacement: "Give me a paraphrase I can verify, not a quote."
steps.note: The goal is not to prove the AI wrong. The goal is to avoid repeating something you cannot stand behind.

steps.title: Hallucination is not drama
steps.body: A hallucination is when an AI generates something false or unsupported as if it were true. It happens because the system is generating likely text, not proving each claim.
steps.mistake: Thinking a citation, title, or quote is real because it is formatted correctly.
steps.good: Ask for uncertainty, sources you can open, and a verification plan before using claims.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is a claim I might use: "[paste claim]". Treat it as unverified. Give me a 4-step plan to check it, tell me what source type would count as strong evidence, and rewrite it in safer language if I cannot verify it.
steps.note: Use this on one claim from homework, a video, or a post.

fields.label: If I cannot verify it, I will...
fields.placeholder: remove it or phrase it as uncertain

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which output is most dangerous to trust without checking?

options.text: A list of brainstormed club names
options.feedback: Low risk. You still choose, but truth is not the main issue.

options.text: A specific quote with a polished citation
options.feedback: Yes. Formatting can look real even when the source is invented.

options.text: A silly analogy for photosynthesis
options.feedback: It might be imperfect, but it is easier to treat as a teaching draft.

lessons.title: Models, tools & agents
lessons.coreQuestion: What is the difference between a model, a tool, and an agent?
lessons.blurb: Separate the brain, the instruments, and the doer before you trust the system.

steps.title: One AI, three different jobs
steps.scenario: An app answers your question, searches the web, and adds a calendar reminder. People call all of it "AI," but those are not the same job.
steps.prompt: Which part is generating, which part is using a tool, and which part is acting for you?

steps.title: Name the part
steps.prompt: Sort each description into the closest bucket.

items.text: Generates a draft email from your instructions
Opens a calculator to solve a precise equation
Searches a website for current ticket prices
Predicts likely next words in a paragraph

steps.reveal: The model generates. Tools fetch or do specific things. Agents combine steps toward a goal.

steps.title: Pick tools for a safe agent
steps.goal: Help plan a study session by checking a calendar, finding open time, and drafting a study checklist.
steps.note: Give an agent only the tools it needs for the job. Extra power is extra risk.

steps.title: Capability comes in layers
steps.body: A model can generate text. A tool can retrieve, calculate, send, edit, or store. An agent uses a model plus tools to pursue a goal through multiple steps.
steps.mistake: Trusting a system more just because it can act in the world.
steps.good: Check the goal, permissions, tools, and stop conditions before letting anything act for you.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: For this task: "[paste a task]", split the AI system into model, tools, and agent behavior. Tell me what permissions are necessary, what permissions would be risky, and where a human should approve before action.
steps.note: Try it with a real task like planning, email, research, or reminders.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What makes an agent different from a plain model response?

options.text: It is always smarter and always safer
options.feedback: No. More ability can mean more risk.

options.text: It can use tools and take steps toward a goal
options.feedback: Right. That is why permissions and approval matter.

options.text: It never needs human review
options.feedback: Opposite. Action usually needs clearer review.

lessons.title: Better follow-ups
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I steer a conversation instead of restarting it?
lessons.blurb: Good AI work is usually not one perfect prompt. It is steering, checking, and narrowing.

steps.title: The answer is almost useful
steps.scenario: You ask AI for help and the answer is not bad, but it is too broad, misses your situation, and gives advice you already knew.
steps.prompt: Do you start over, or do you steer it?

steps.title: Restart or follow up?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether it throws away context or improves the current conversation.

items.text: “Never mind. Give me a better answer.”
“Use the same plan, but make it fit a 20-minute study session.”
“That is too generic. Ask me 3 questions before revising.”
Opening a new chat every time the first answer is imperfect

steps.reveal: A follow-up keeps useful context and adds direction. Restarting often loses what the model already learned about the task.

steps.title: Turn frustration into steering
steps.weak: That answer is bad. Try again.
steps.strong: Keep the 3-part structure, but make it specific to someone studying after school for 25 minutes. Add one example for each part, and end by asking me what constraint you may have missed.

steps.title: Conversation is control
steps.body: A good AI conversation is a loop: ask, inspect, steer, verify, then use. Follow-ups are how you turn a generic answer into something that fits.
steps.mistake: Treating the first answer as the final answer.
steps.good: Name what to keep, what to change, what to add, and what to check.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is an AI answer I almost like: [paste answer]. Help me improve it with 4 follow-ups: one to narrow it, one to make it more concrete, one to check assumptions, and one to make the final output easier to use.
steps.note: This works best when the first answer is close, not useless.

fields.label: Keep
fields.placeholder: what was useful in the first answer

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which follow-up gives you the most control?

options.text: “Make it better.”
options.feedback: Too vague. The model has to guess what better means.

options.text: “Keep the structure, make it fit my 20-minute limit, and ask one question if a constraint is missing.”
options.feedback: Right. It says what to keep, change, and check.

options.text: “Start over from scratch.”
options.feedback: Sometimes useful, but it usually throws away helpful context.

lessons.title: Roles, formats & constraints
lessons.coreQuestion: How do roles and formats change what I get back?
lessons.blurb: Role, format, and constraints are control knobs. Use them deliberately.

steps.title: Same topic, different answer
steps.scenario: Ask for “help with my presentation” and you get generic advice. Ask for a skeptical reviewer, a slide outline, and a 5-minute limit, and the answer changes completely.
steps.prompt: Which part changed the answer most: role, format, or constraint?

steps.title: Name the control knob
steps.prompt: Sort each prompt part by what it controls.

items.text: Act as a skeptical science fair judge
Return a 6-slide outline
Use no more than 120 words
Be a patient tutor who asks before explaining

steps.reveal: Role changes the lens. Format changes the shape. Constraints set boundaries.

steps.title: Add the missing controls
steps.weak: Help me with my history project.
steps.strong: Act as a history project coach. Format: give me a 5-part outline with one question under each part. Constraints: do not write the final paragraphs, keep it at 9th-grade level, and flag any claim that needs a source. Success check: end with what I should do next myself.

steps.title: Roles are not costumes
steps.body: A role is useful when it changes what the model pays attention to: tutor, reviewer, planner, debate opponent, editor. A format is useful when it makes the output easier to inspect.
steps.mistake: Adding a fancy role but no task, no constraints, and no check.
steps.good: Use role + task + format + constraints + success check.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Take this task: [paste task]. Give me 3 prompt versions using different roles: tutor, critic, and project manager. For each, choose a format and one constraint that would make the answer easier to use.
steps.note: Compare the answers. The best role depends on the job.

fields.label: Success check
fields.placeholder: how I know the answer is useful

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the safest prompt pattern?

options.text: A dramatic role with no task details
options.feedback: A role alone does not create control.

options.text: Role + task + format + constraints + success check
options.feedback: Yes. That combination gives both direction and review.

options.text: The longest prompt possible
options.feedback: Length is not the same as structure.

lessons.title: Getting AI to teach you
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I make AI a tutor, not an answer vending machine?
lessons.blurb: A tutor makes you think. An answer machine lets you skip the work.

steps.title: The homework shortcut trap
steps.scenario: You ask AI for the answer, understand it for two seconds, then cannot solve the next problem alone.
steps.prompt: What would a good tutor do differently?

steps.title: Tutor move or answer-machine move?
steps.prompt: Sort the AI behaviors by whether they protect your learning.

items.text: Ask what I already tried before explaining
Give the final answer immediately
Give one hint, then wait for my attempt
Write the whole assignment in my voice

steps.reveal: A tutor creates effort at the right moment. Too much help can feel good and still weaken learning.

steps.title: Repair the tutor prompt
steps.strong: Act as a tutor. Do not give the final answer first. Ask me what I tried, give one hint at a time, wait for my attempt, then check my reasoning and give a similar practice problem.

steps.title: Learning needs friction
steps.body: The best AI tutor does not remove all struggle. It adjusts the struggle: hints before answers, questions before lectures, practice before confidence.
steps.mistake: Confusing “I read the answer” with “I can do it myself.”
steps.good: Ask AI to question, hint, test, and correct you without taking over.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Teach me [topic]. Start by asking what I already know. Give me one hint at a time, do not reveal the full answer until I try, and end with a short quiz plus one transfer problem.
steps.note: Use this when the goal is learning, not just finishing.

fields.label: Proof I learned it
fields.placeholder: I can solve a similar problem alone

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which request turns AI into a better tutor?

options.text: “Give me the answer so I can submit it.”
options.feedback: That finishes the task but skips the learning.

options.text: “Give one hint, wait for my attempt, then check my reasoning.”
options.feedback: Right. That keeps you doing the important thinking.

options.text: “Explain everything for 20 paragraphs.”
options.feedback: More explanation is not always better. Practice and feedback matter.

lessons.title: Human agency
lessons.coreQuestion: Where must a human stay in the loop?
lessons.blurb: Use AI for help, but keep the goal, values, and final decision human.

steps.title: The AI sounds sure
steps.scenario: An AI recommends which club you should quit, which class you should take, and how to apologize to a friend. The advice sounds calm and reasonable.
steps.prompt: Which part can AI help with, and which part should stay yours?

steps.title: AI helper or human decision?
steps.prompt: Sort each task by whether AI can help or whether the human must own the final decision.

items.text: List possible tradeoffs before choosing a class
Decide what matters most to your family or values
Draft three respectful ways to start a hard conversation
Choose whether to forgive someone

steps.reveal: AI can widen your thinking. It should not replace your responsibility for values, relationships, and consequences.

steps.title: Put the human back in charge
steps.weak: Tell me what I should do.
steps.strong: Help me think through this decision without deciding for me. Decision: [describe]. Options: [list]. Values I care about: [list]. Give tradeoffs, questions I should ask, and what information is missing. Do not tell me the final choice.

steps.title: Agency is not anti-AI
steps.body: Human agency means you use AI as a thinking aid while keeping ownership of goals, values, consent, and final action. The safer pattern is: AI suggests, human judges.
steps.mistake: Treating confident advice as permission to stop deciding.
steps.good: Ask for options, consequences, missing information, and counterarguments before you choose.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: I have a decision: [describe]. Do not decide for me. Give me 3 options, tradeoffs for each, what information is missing, and 5 questions that help me make the decision myself.
steps.note: Use this for low-risk decisions first, then notice how much better the conversation gets.

fields.label: Before acting, I will...
fields.placeholder: pause, check, ask a person, decide myself

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which use keeps human agency strongest?

options.text: Ask AI to choose for you because it sounds objective
options.feedback: That gives away the final judgment.

options.text: Ask AI for options, tradeoffs, and missing information, then decide yourself
options.feedback: Right. AI supports the thinking, not the ownership.

options.text: Avoid AI for every decision, even low-risk planning
options.feedback: Agency is not avoidance. It is controlled use.

lessons.title: Verification & sources
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I check a claim without trusting the AI’s word?
lessons.blurb: Turn “sounds right” into a source check you can defend.

steps.title: The source that might not exist
steps.scenario: AI gives you a statistic, a title, and a link-looking citation. It fits your argument perfectly.
steps.prompt: What do you check before you repeat it?

steps.title: Source strength
steps.prompt: Sort each source move by whether it is strong enough for a real claim.

items.text: A citation name that only appears in the AI answer
The original report, paper, textbook, or official page
A screenshot with no date or source
Two reliable sources that agree on the same specific fact

steps.reveal: A source is not strong because it is formatted. It is strong because you can open it, inspect it, and explain why it fits.

steps.title: Check the claim
steps.claim: Students learn 50% faster when every homework assignment uses AI.
steps: Ask what exact claim is being made.
Search for the original source, not just summaries.
Check who published it, when, and what was actually measured.
Rewrite the claim more carefully if the evidence is weak or narrower than the sentence.
steps.note: The safest move is often not “true or false.” It is “what can I responsibly say?”

steps.title: Verification is a habit
steps.body: AI can help you plan a check, but it cannot be the only witness. For claims that matter, you need source type, date, author or organization, and fit to your exact sentence.
steps.mistake: Using a source because it supports your point, not because it is reliable.
steps.good: Verify the claim, then shrink or revise it until it matches the evidence.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Here is a claim: [paste claim]. Build a verification plan. Tell me what source type would be strong, what would be weak, and give me a safer sentence if I cannot verify the full claim.
steps.note: Use this before essays, presentations, posts, or project claims.

fields.label: Claim
fields.placeholder: the exact sentence I might use

fields.label: Safer rewrite
fields.placeholder: what I can say if evidence is limited

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What should you do with an AI citation before using it?

options.text: Trust it if the title sounds real
options.feedback: Fake citations can sound completely real.

options.text: Open and inspect the source, then make sure it supports the exact claim
options.feedback: Right. Verification means checking source and fit.

options.text: Ask AI to promise that it is real
options.feedback: A promise is not evidence.

lessons.title: Bias, fairness & perspective
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I spot bias in an AI answer?
lessons.blurb: Bias often hides in loaded words, missing groups, and one-sided framing.

steps.title: The answer sounds neutral
steps.scenario: AI summarizes a debate and says one side is “reasonable” while the other is “emotional.” It never explains why.
steps.prompt: What words or missing perspectives would you inspect first?

steps.title: Bias signal or fair move?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether it helps fairness or signals possible bias.

items.text: Using loaded labels without evidence
Naming what evidence would change the answer
Ignoring the group most affected by the decision
Showing the strongest argument from more than one side

steps.reveal: Fairness starts with noticing framing: who is named, who is missing, and which words carry judgment.

steps.title: Spot the loaded language
steps.passage: The responsible students wanted reasonable AI rules, but the lazy students complained because restrictions would expose their shortcuts.
steps.reveal: You caught the framing words. They push you toward a judgment before evidence appears.

steps.title: Bias is not only being mean
steps.body: Bias can be obvious, but it can also be a missing perspective, a loaded comparison, a hidden assumption, or a pattern copied from flawed data.
steps.mistake: Calling an answer fair just because it sounds calm.
steps.good: Ask who is missing, what assumptions are being made, and how the answer changes under another perspective.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Review this AI answer for bias: [paste answer]. Look for loaded words, missing perspectives, hidden assumptions, and what evidence would make the answer fairer. Then rewrite it more neutrally.
steps.note: This is useful for summaries, debates, policies, and recommendations.

fields.label: Missing perspective
fields.placeholder: who is affected but not represented

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which is the best first bias check?

options.text: See if the answer sounds polite
options.feedback: Polite wording can still carry biased framing.

options.text: Look for loaded words, missing perspectives, and hidden assumptions
options.feedback: Right. Those are practical things you can inspect.

options.text: Assume AI has no bias because it is a computer
options.feedback: No. Models can reflect biased data and biased prompts.

lessons.title: Privacy & personal data
lessons.coreQuestion: What should I never paste into an AI tool?
lessons.blurb: Good AI habits include knowing what not to share.

steps.title: The convenient paste
steps.scenario: You want AI to rewrite an email, so you paste the whole thread. It includes names, phone numbers, a private problem, and a school account detail.
steps.prompt: Which parts should have been removed first?

steps.title: Paste or protect?
steps.prompt: Sort what is usually safer to share versus what should be removed or anonymized.

items.text: A made-up example sentence
Someone’s full name plus private situation
A general task description with no identifying details
Passwords, tokens, addresses, or private account details

steps.reveal: The safest prompt often uses a fake example, initials, or a summary instead of raw private data.

steps.title: Anonymize the request
steps.weak: Rewrite this message from Maya to Mr. Chen about her medical appointment: [private thread].
steps.strong: Rewrite a short message from a student to a teacher asking to reschedule because of a private appointment. Do not include names, medical details, addresses, or account information. Tone: respectful and brief.

steps.title: Privacy is part of skill
steps.body: Before using AI, decide what data the tool does not need. Names, locations, passwords, health details, private conflicts, and account information usually do not belong in prompts.
steps.mistake: Thinking “I am only asking for wording” means private context is safe to paste.
steps.good: Summarize, anonymize, or use a fake example when the exact private details are not needed.

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: Help me rewrite this request without using private details. First ask me what information can be anonymized. Then create a safe version of the prompt before answering.
steps.note: Do this before pasting messages, documents, screenshots, or personal stories.

fields.label: Before sending, I will check for...

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What is the safest way to ask AI for help with a private message?

options.text: Paste the full thread because the AI needs context
options.feedback: Often it does not need the private details.

options.text: Summarize the situation and remove names, secrets, and identifying details
options.feedback: Right. Give only what the task needs.

options.text: Paste it, then ask AI not to remember it
options.feedback: Do not rely on that. Protect before sending.

lessons.title: When not to use AI
lessons.coreQuestion: When is the right move to NOT use AI?
lessons.blurb: Sometimes the strongest AI skill is choosing a human, a source, or your own effort.

steps.title: The fastest tool is not always the right tool
steps.scenario: You can use AI to reply to a friend, solve a practice problem, summarize a sensitive story, or make a medical guess. Fast does not mean wise.
steps.prompt: Which one would you avoid first, and why?

steps.title: Use AI or pause?
steps.prompt: Sort the situations by whether AI can help or whether you should pause and use another route.

items.text: Brainstorming possible titles for a club poster
Entering someone’s private story with names and identifying details
Getting hints on a practice problem without final answers
Making a medical, legal, or safety decision from AI alone

steps.reveal: AI is strongest when the risk is low, the human stays in charge, and you can verify. Pause when privacy, safety, law, health, or relationships are at stake.

steps.title: Build the pause routine
steps.goal: Decide whether to use AI on a sensitive task.
correct: Remove private details if AI is still useful
Choose a trusted source or person when stakes are high
Use AI only for low-risk framing or questions
steps.note: The pause routine keeps speed from overriding judgment.

steps.title: Not using AI is not falling behind
steps.body: The goal is not to use AI everywhere. The goal is to know when it helps, when it weakens learning, and when another source or person is safer.
steps.mistake: Using AI because it is available, not because it fits the risk.
steps.good: Ask: What is the cost of being wrong, what data would I expose, and who should decide?

steps.title: Try it for real
steps.prompt: For this task: [paste task]. Help me decide whether to use AI. Rate the privacy risk, learning risk, accuracy risk, and human-relationship risk. If I should not use AI, suggest a safer next step.
steps.note: This makes AI help with the decision about AI, while you still choose.

fields.label: Better next step
fields.placeholder: ask teacher, check source, try myself

fields.label: If I use AI, only for...

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: When should you avoid relying on AI alone?

options.text: When the stakes involve health, safety, law, privacy, or a relationship
options.feedback: Right. Use a trusted source, person, or your own judgment.

options.text: Whenever you need a brainstorm list
options.feedback: Low-risk brainstorming can be a good use.

options.text: Only when the AI says it is uncertain
options.feedback: You need to judge the risk yourself, not wait for the model.

lessons.title: From prompt to workflow
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I chain prompts into a repeatable workflow?
lessons.blurb: Turn a repeated AI task into a small system with inputs, checks, saved output, and a human approval point.

steps.title: The repeated-task problem
steps.scenario: You keep asking AI to help with the same kind of task: summarize notes, make a study plan, check a draft, or turn ideas into a project outline. Each time, you rewrite the prompt from scratch.
steps.prompt: A workflow is how you stop starting over. It turns one useful prompt into a repeatable path.

steps.title: Sort the pieces
steps.prompt: Decide whether each piece is a one-off prompt, a workflow step, or unsafe automation.

items.text: “Explain this paragraph.”
Collect the input before asking AI to transform it.
Send the AI answer automatically without anyone checking it.
Compare the output against a rubric before saving it.

steps.reveal: A workflow is not more magic. It is a safer sequence of small steps.

steps.title: Build the safe order
steps.goal: Create a repeatable workflow for turning messy class notes into a useful study guide.
correct: Ask AI for a first draft
Decide what still needs human review
steps.note: The order matters because AI output should be inspected before it becomes something you rely on.

steps.title: What changed?
steps.body: A prompt asks for one answer. A workflow defines the input, the AI job, the check, the saved artifact, and the human approval point. That is how you begin building with AI instead of only chatting with it.
steps.mistake: Skipping the check step because the AI answer sounds polished.
steps.good: Make the check part of the workflow so quality is not optional.

fields.label: Repeated task
fields.placeholder: Example: turn notes into a study guide

fields.label: Input needed
fields.placeholder: What you give the AI first

fields.label: Verification check
fields.placeholder: How you catch weak or wrong output

fields.label: Human approval point
fields.placeholder: What you decide before using it

steps.title: Exit check
steps.question: Which version is a real workflow?

options.text: Ask AI to “make it better” until it sounds good
options.feedback: That is still a loose conversation, not a repeatable path.

options.text: Input → AI draft → check → revise → save → human approval
options.feedback: Right. The workflow includes checks and a decision point.

options.text: Let AI receive, rewrite, and send everything automatically
options.feedback: That removes the safety and judgment steps.
